content_voiceover: This graph is the confirmatory test for pseudothrombocytopenia, and it's a classic board figure. It plots measured platelet count over four hours for the same blood sample drawn into two different anticoagulants, EDTA in dark blue and sodium citrate in pink. Both start around the same baseline, roughly 190 to 200 thousand, but look what happens over time. The EDTA sample crashes rapidly, dropping to about 60 thousand by one hour and settling near 40 thousand by four hours, because ongoing EDTA-mediated clumping keeps consuming countable single platelets. The citrate sample declines much more gently, staying above 120 thousand even at four hours, because citrate doesn't expose that same cryptic GPIIb-IIIa epitope the way EDTA does. The clinical application is straightforward and testable, if you see an unexpectedly low platelet count with no bleeding symptoms, redraw the sample into a sodium citrate tube, or alternatively do a fresh fingerstick smear, and if the citrate or fingerstick count comes back substantially higher, you've confirmed EDTA-induced pseudothrombocytopenia rather than true thrombocytopenia, and you can spare the patient an unnecessary workup.
keypoints: EDTA sample: platelet count crashes to ~40k by 4 hours
Sodium citrate sample: stays above 120k over same time period
Divergence confirms EDTA-dependent clumping, not true thrombocytopenia
Fix: redraw in citrate tube or do a fresh fingerstick smear
Correct low count on repeat testing → avoid unnecessary ITP workup
keypoint_voiceover: This graph is your confirmatory test. Same blood sample, two tubes, over four hours the EDTA tube crashes down to around forty thousand platelets while the citrate tube barely drifts, staying above one hundred twenty thousand. That gap confirms EDTA-dependent clumping rather than real thrombocytopenia. Practically, if you see a surprising low platelet count with no bleeding, redraw in citrate or do a fingerstick smear, and a normal repeat count saves the patient from an unnecessary bone marrow biopsy or steroid course.
